subject: chemistry

moments.title: Pauling introduces resonance and hybridisation
moments.body:
Pauling publishes a paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society titled 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond. Application of Results Obtained from the Quantum Mechanics and from a Theory of Paramagnetic Susceptibility to the Structure of Molecules.'

He introduces the concept of hybridised atomic orbitals (sp, sp2, sp3) and resonance between Lewis structures. Both ideas become standard chemistry within a decade.
moments.takeaway: Quantum mechanics is brought into structural chemistry. Bonding becomes describable in orbital language.

moments.title: Electronegativity scale
moments.body:
Pauling derives a numerical scale of electronegativity from bond dissociation energies. The most electronegative element (fluorine) gets 4.0; the least (caesium) about 0.7. Differences in electronegativity predict bond polarity quantitatively.

The scale becomes universal. Every chemistry textbook still uses Pauling electronegativity values.
moments.takeaway: A simple number summarises a deep chemical property. Electronegativity becomes a workhorse of structural prediction.

moments.title: The Nature of the Chemical Bond (book)
moments.body:
Pauling publishes the book version of his ideas: The Nature of the Chemical Bond. It integrates resonance, hybridisation, electronegativity, partial ionic character and crystal structure into one framework. It becomes one of the most-cited science books of the 20th century.

The book is still in print and is the foundation of how chemists talk about bonds today.

quote.text: The chemical bond, as we now know, is the most important thing in molecular structure.
quote.attrib: Linus Pauling, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, 1939

moments.takeaway: A single book systematises bonding for the entire field. Generations of chemists learn from it.

moments.title: Two Nobel Prizes
moments.body:
Pauling wins the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry 'for his research into the nature of the chemical bond.' He is the sole recipient.

In 1962 he wins the Nobel Peace Prize for his campaign against atmospheric nuclear weapons testing. He had personally lobbied governments and gathered signatures from over 11,000 scientists. The 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty was partly the result. He remains one of only four people to win two Nobel Prizes — and the only one to have won both unshared.
moments.takeaway: Two Nobels, in different fields, both unshared. A scientist's public conscience can also be world-changing.

now.title: Bonding theory today
now.body:
Pauling's valence bond theory coexists with molecular orbital theory, which is generally more accurate for delocalised systems. Modern computational chemistry uses density functional theory (DFT) and ab initio methods to predict bond properties from first principles.

Electronegativity remains a useful concept, though it has been redefined several times (Mulliken, Allred-Rochow, Allen) on different theoretical bases. Pauling's empirical values still appear in most textbooks.
now.open_questions: Can DFT functionals be designed to handle all bonds correctly without empirical adjustment? How well can we predict properties of materials and biomolecules from quantum mechanics alone? Are there bond types that still resist quantum-mechanical description?

reflection: Pauling's later years included a famous wrong turn — his unshakeable advocacy of high-dose vitamin C as a cure for everything from colds to cancer, which clinical trials repeatedly failed to support. A great scientist can still be powerfully wrong. How should the discipline weigh a lifetime's achievement against late-career errors?
